A.reason: All candidates are usable. Primary mechanisms are centralized return processing (0,5), visible shelving destinations (1), an on-site reserve (2), optional repair of existing disorder (3), reader condition screening (4), and a departure-time borrowing cue (6). Candidate 5 repairs candidate 0 rather than introducing a new mechanism. It is strongest because it specifies overflow handling, interrupted processing, workload limits and a simpler fallback, while checking availability, condition, cleanup and seated access.

B.reason: All candidates are usable. Primary mechanisms are centralized return processing (0), visible shelving destinations (1), an on-site reserve (2), optional repair of existing disorder (3), and portable return reminders (4). Candidate 1 best combines immediate book availability with distributed tidying, optional classification, volunteer condition checks and a pilot that tests whether sorting consumes the saved effort. Candidate 3's invitation to handle damaged books warrants clearer boundaries but is not a definite serious hard-constraint violation.

pair.reason: A5 narrowly beats B1 on operational feasibility and inspectability: it provides explicit responses to box overflow and unfinished work within the fixed volunteer allowance. B1 offers a plausible self-maintaining ritual, but its category maintenance adds work and its return-box capacity response is less developed. Neither proposal has demonstrated effects.
